label: rem:gluon-stabiliser-ledger
title: The gluon ledger: what step 4 enumerates, and why the trefoil loses
html:
Remark. The gluon ledger: what step 4 enumerates, and why the trefoil loses

Step 4 of the derived atom says the integer LP dual "selects the minimum gluon", and the proton block says it "enumerates all feasible gluon combinations and selects the configuration minimizing |\mathrm{tr}_M|". Neither says what the enumeration ranges over. This remark says it. The answer dissolves the question it was written to settle: nothing is excluded, so no exclusion argument is owed.

The feasible set. The universal ILP fixes it. The stabiliser K ranges over non-trivial braid words up to a crossing cap; the constraint is Frobenius positivity of the resulting state, G\cdot\mathrm{NF}(x\cdot K)\ge 0; the objective is minimum crossing number with |\mathrm{tr}_M(x\cdot K)| as tiebreak. The producer behind the nucleon numbers enumerates words over \{\sigma_0,\sigma_1,L_+,L_-\} of length at most three — 4 + 4^2 + 4^3 = 84 candidates, which is the count the unwrap-depth remark reports for the proton at baryon level. So the range is not "combinations of L_\pm". It is every braid word inside the cap, and the four-letter alphabet composes to all six normal-form basis words, e^- included.

The trefoil is inside it. The natural worry is why the stabiliser may not be e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0: it is a basis word exactly as L_\pm are, and like them it has \mathrm{Vol} = 0, so nothing topological separates them. It is not excluded. As a three-letter braid word it sits in the enumeration — reached as \sigma_0\cdot L_-, or as L_+\cdot\sigma_0 — and it is admissible: applied to either bare nucleon it leaves the state Frobenius-positive. It loses, and it loses under either objective the corpus states. On |\mathrm{tr}_M| it is beaten by an order of magnitude or more for both nucleons. On crossing count it costs three, and both nucleons have admissible stabilisers costing one or two. That is a defeat in the minimisation, not a prohibition, and it is the only answer the construction supports.

Lepton number is not the reason. It would be a tidy story — e^- is the lepton channel, so admitting it changes lepton number — but the framework's own definition refuses it. Categorical lepton number counts Skein smoothings, and its properties state that the Iwahori–Hecke algebra contains no mechanism to change it: violation "requires a process that changes crossing type without passing through the Skein relation". Gluon stabilisation is Hecke multiplication followed by Gröbner–Shirshov reduction. It smooths nothing, so \Delta L = 0 for every candidate, e^- among them. The conservation table agrees by construction: it carries no row for step 4 at all, and it assigns L = 0 to a nucleon whose normal form is dominated by e^-\approx +1.02 — a coefficient the same block calls the beta-decay channel, not a lepton. An e^- weight in a Hecke normal form is an amplitude. Reading it as a lepton would forbid the output the proton block already asserts.

Nor is double counting. The Hopf gluon does redistribute normal-form weight from \sigma_1 into the trefoil channel, so e^- is the output of stabilisation. That is a consequence of the selection, not a constraint on the search: an e^- input would be a different, worse candidate, not a quantity counted twice.

Hyperbolic volume decides nothing here. Where a competing channel carries a hyperbolic constituent, volume settles the selection outright — the Borromean rings carry 8G and a torus link carries none. That is what happens one step earlier, at the antiquark disposal, and the antiquark ledger works it out. That route is unavailable at step 4. All five non-identity basis words are torus-type with \mathrm{Vol} = 0, so volume separates none of them, and the whole selection falls to \mathrm{tr}_M and crossing count.

What is genuinely unsettled is the crossing count, not the feasible set.

The proton takes two gluon crossings and the neutron four, and that difference is what makes the neutron heavier and so feeds \mathfrak{Q}_\beta. The neutron's gluon count is two, not four. The neutron block records eleven crossings in total — six from \mathcal{B}_3, three from quarks, two from gluons — since its stated \mathrm{net}(\mathfrak{n}) = +0.7976 is the eleven-crossing value on the k-ladder, the thirteen-crossing value being 1.2359. The proton block applies a single Hopf link L_- = \sigma_1\sigma_0, also two. The two nucleons therefore carry the same gluon-crossing count, so the struck sentence's premise does not hold, and whatever carries \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{n}} - \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{p}} is not this difference.

The disagreement that survives is narrower. The universal ILP's own witness records the gluon as a single \sigma_1 at one crossing; its instantiation table records \sigma_0\sigma_0 at two; the proton block records L_- = \sigma_1\sigma_0 at two; the neutron block records two. Four statements of one quantity, two answers. The spread is not a rounding difference: under the minimum-crossing objective the universal ILP states, a one-crossing stabiliser strictly beats a two-crossing one, so the two readings are not both selections of the same rule.

The feasible set is well defined and e^- is fairly beaten inside it; which stabiliser the stated objective actually selects is a separate open question, on which the mass split depends.
